On 2023-05-26, the user asked for 10 bullet points summarizing a supplied Barron’s interview titled “Why Famed Value Investor Bill Miller Is Still Bullish on Bitcoin, Amazon Stock, and More.”

In the supplied interview, investor Bill Miller, age 72, said he planned to step down from managing public money at the end of 2022, while remaining engaged in markets. His son, Bill Miller IV, was to take over the firm’s income-fund business, and Samantha McLemore was buying the Opportunity Trust business. Miller said he would own 25% of both pieces and be the largest investor in both funds, but did not want responsibility for managing other people’s money.

Bill Miller said stocks were cheap and investors with a horizon longer than about a year would probably do fine because the U.S. economy grows over time. He argued that the Federal Reserve had first underestimated inflation and then likely overreacted by raising rates; he said experienced inflation was falling rapidly.

Bill Miller defined investment value as the present value of future free cash flows, not as a low price-to-earnings ratio or high dividend yield. Amazon was his largest personal holding by far; he said Amazon traded around $85 in the interview, versus $170 a year earlier, and predicted it could be difficult for the stock not to double over three years because of cash generated by Amazon Web Services and advertising.

Bill Miller named Delta Air Lines, Chesapeake Energy, OneMain Holdings, Quad/Graphics, Gannett, Clear Secure, and Farfetch among his favored stocks. He cited Delta’s 10% free-cash-flow yield, Chesapeake’s secure 10% dividend yield, OneMain’s 11% dividend yield, Quad/Graphics trading near $3.50, Gannett’s prospective free cash flow equal to half its market capitalization over 12 months, and Farfetch trading near $4. He had an investment interest in Clear Secure and had been an early investor and board member.

Bill Miller distinguished Bitcoin, which he viewed as a possible store of value like digital gold, from other cryptocurrencies, which he grouped as speculative venture investments that mostly would fail. He called Bitcoin a “sound speculation,” said a person could consider putting at least 1% of net worth into it, and expected Bitcoin could do well if the Federal Reserve began easing monetary policy. He personally owned Bitcoin and also held it in some private accounts.

Bill Miller said he had recently bought more Amazon shares and bought Silvergate Capital a week before the interview; he expected to buy more Coinbase. He also owned Coinbase and Silvergate, describing Coinbase as a transparent, U.S.-based, dominant crypto company and Silvergate as an FDIC-insured bank subject to banking regulations. He generally preferred inaction and said he rarely sold holdings unless forced by margin calls.

In retirement, Bill Miller expected to travel more, return to Baltimore for the Orioles’ Opening Day, remain active in philanthropy, and focus giving on education and science. He said he would be more active with the Santa Fe Institute and was on the Johns Hopkins University board and its investment committee; he had also started a foundation. Miller said he would consider the Baltimore Orioles if they came up for sale, but saw a major opportunity in women’s basketball.

The assistant’s 10-bullet summary incorrectly said Miller’s Opportunity Trust lost 37% in 2021; the supplied interview says it lost 37% “this year,” referring to the article’s 2022 context. The assistant also introduced NFL and NBA as possible investments, although Miller specifically mentioned an opportunity in women’s basketball, and it attributed an explicit prediction that the stock market would be higher in 2023 that Miller did not make in the supplied text.
